activity_context.topic_title: Integration by Substitution With Inverse Trigonometric Functions

examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Secant
examples.worked_solution:
This resembles the basic integral for $\textrm{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

Let $u = 5x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=5
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
5\,\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5\,\text{d}x}{|5x|\sqrt{(5x)^{2}-1}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec}(u)+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(5x)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{36\cdot (1+{x}^{2}/36)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}/36}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/6)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{6})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{6}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{6}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=6\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{36+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{12}\int \frac{1}{1+(x/6)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (6\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{6})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
